entry.title: Rust Proposes Exposing Internal "Places" to Enable Flexible Smart Pointers
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | lwn.net | source | discussion

Rust's language team is developing a design to make user-defined smart pointers as flexible as built-in references. Currently, smart pointers like `MutexGuard` cannot always be used in complex patterns where native references succeed—such as with the `HashMap` `entry` API—because the borrow checker cannot track their internal structure. This limitation often requires developers to employ unintuitive reborrowing techniques to satisfy the compiler.

The proposed approach involves exposing the compiler's internal concept of a "place" to user code through new handle types and traits including `ReadPlace`, `WritePlace`, `ProjectPlace`, and `BorrowPlace`. By implementing these traits, library authors can explicitly instruct the borrow checker on how to handle custom pointer types, which could eventually support features like pattern matching and destructive pattern matching for smart pointers.

entry.title: Zeroization Practices Can Unintentionally Increase Secret Exposure in Memory
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | 00f.net | discussion

Zeroization, the practice of wiping sensitive data from memory, can inadvertently create additional, unmanaged copies of secrets in stack or register space. Compiler optimizations often discard standard `memset()` calls or trigger the creation of new stack spills when using opaque wiping functions, leaving the original secret intact in registers or other memory locations.

These residual copies increase the risk of information leakage through core dumps, hibernation files, and microarchitectural vulnerabilities. Effective sanitization requires analyzing optimized machine code and register usage rather than blindly applying wiping functions to local variables.

entry.title: Rat Rewrites Register Allocator Using Priority Bin-Packing
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | hexrat.cc | discussion

The rat compiler backend has transitioned from a 1392-line linear scan register allocator to a 584-line priority bin-packing allocator. The new system maps x86-64 virtual registers to physical general-purpose or XMM registers, or spills them to the stack when no registers are free.

The allocator employs a five-step process: numbering live ranges, marking fixed registers, coalescing bundles, picking registers by priority, and spilling. Performance testing against the previous implementation shows significant efficiency gains, including a 77% reduction in allocator time and a 43% reduction in total compilation time when compiling SQLite.

entry.content:

Applying the modulo operator to a large random number to select items from a set creates modulo bias, causing non-uniform probability distributions where certain outcomes are more likely. This occurs when the range of the random number source is not a multiple of the size of the set.

Developers typically employ a pair of stacks—an undo stack and a redo stack—to handle action history in a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) manner. By popping actions from the undo stack and pushing them onto the redo stack, applications allow users to navigate through a reversible history of changes.

The technical requirements vary by application type, with text editors requiring significantly less overhead than bitmap graphics programs. Text editors can store simple character changes, whereas bitmap editors must often take snapshots of large segments of image data to allow for pixel-level restoration. This creates a trade-off between the depth of the undo history and the consumption of system memory and disk space.

Converting IPv4 addresses to IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses via Go's netip.Addr type is currently eight times slower than a native implementation. This performance gap occurs because the Go compiler does not optimize the netip.AddrFrom16(ip.As16()) pattern that developers must use to compensate for the lack of a dedicated Map() method in the standard library.

Optimization strategies include modifying the Go standard library, using the unsafe package, or implementing a compiler-level hack. The latter approach involves intercepting the conversion pattern during the compiler's noding phase and replacing it with an efficient, direct struct assignment within the intermediate representation.

entry.content:

Rust's `#[derive]` attribute for traits such as `Debug`, `Display`, and `Clone` automatically generates code containing `#[inline]` hints. This behavior is implied in the Rust Reference and can be verified by expanding the macros.

While inlining is beneficial for trivial implementations, it can cause significant binary size increases when used with complex or deeply nested structures like large error hierarchies. Replacing standard `#[derive]` with a custom macro that applies `#[inline(never)]` can mitigate this bloat, as seen in a case where the `uv` binary size was reduced by 160KB.
